summary:
Crew Self-Check is a health monitoring app that helps astronauts on long-duration missions spot health changes in themselves and act on them without waiting for Earth. Each day the astronaut logs mood, stress, sleep, exercise, resting heart rate, and symptoms. The software compares these against their personal baseline and rates five areas as Nominal, Watch, or Alert: heart and circulation, bones and muscle, immune system, mind and mood, and radiation and air quality. These areas map to the challenge’s hazards: radiation, isolation, altered gravity, and a closed environment.

For every area, the app explains why it flagged a change and gives a concrete next step, such as adding resistive exercise, booking a behavioral health call, or moving to the storm shelter. It also projects radiation dose to mission end and generates a report the astronaut can send to the flight surgeon.

This matters because on missions to Mars, communication delays of up to 20 minutes each way make real-time medical support impossible. Catching small trends early, such as slow bone loss, creeping stress, or rising heart rate, prevents serious problems and keeps crews mission-ready.

(Word count: about 175)

details:
Crew Self-Check: Project Details

What it does and how it works

Crew Self-Check is a web app that helps an astronaut monitor their own health on a long mission. Each day the astronaut completes a short check-in: mood, stress, sleep, exercise minutes, resting heart rate from a wearable, contact outside the crew, and any symptoms.

The software compares the last few days with that astronaut's own baseline. It rates five areas as Nominal, Watch or Alert:

  • Heart and circulation: resting heart rate, palpitations and dizziness, linked to fluid shifts in microgravity.
  • Bones and muscle: exercise levels, back pain and a rough estimate of monthly bone loss.
  • Immune system: sleep, rashes and cold-type symptoms.
  • Mind and mood: mood, stress, irritability and isolation.
  • Radiation and air: career radiation dose projected to mission end, cabin CO₂ and headaches.

Each card shows a 30-day trend, the reason for its rating and a concrete next step. A "what to do today" list is sorted by severity. The app also writes a report the astronaut can copy and send to the flight surgeon. Demo buttons simulate three weeks of strain, a solar storm and a CO₂ fault.

Benefits

  • Catches slow changes early, such as creeping stress, falling exercise or rising heart rate.
  • Works when Earth can't answer quickly. Mars communication delays can reach about 20 minutes each way.
  • Compares against each person's own normal, which reduces false alarms. For example, exercise doesn't trigger a heart-rate alert.
  • Gives plain-language guidance and shows the reason for every rating, so astronauts can trust and check it.
  • Gives the flight surgeon a ready summary instead of a raw data dump.

Intended impact

The goal is to make astronauts active partners in their own medical care, which will matter more as missions go to the Moon and Mars. Healthier crews are safer and keep missions on track. The same approach could help people in remote or isolated settings on Earth, such as polar stations, submarines and rural clinics.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks. The app is one self-contained file.
  • Design: responsive layout with light and dark themes, keyboard focus styles, and status shown by text labels as well as color.
  • Fonts: Barlow and Barlow Semi Condensed from Google Fonts.
  • Development: built with Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant, and published as a hosted web page. The demo deck was made with Claude's slide tool.
  • Hardware: none. The prototype runs in any modern browser, and all readings are simulated.

Creativity

  • The astronaut is the primary user, not mission control. Most health dashboards are built for ground teams.
  • It links each space hazard to a body system and an action, not just a chart.
  • It looks ahead by projecting radiation dose to mission end, so the astronaut sees a limit coming before reaching it.
  • It treats mental health and sleep as seriously as heart rate.
  • It includes an escalation path for when ground can't reply in time.

Factors we considered

  • Delay and autonomy: advice has to work without real-time ground support.
  • Personalization: each astronaut has a different baseline, so alerts show change from their own normal.
  • Alert fatigue: a three-level system with context, such as exercise, keeps alerts meaningful.
  • Privacy: health data is sensitive, so we plan a private-by-default mode where the astronaut chooses what to share.
  • Honesty about limits: the data is simulated, thresholds are illustrative and bone-loss figures are estimates. It is decision support, not a medical device.
  • Future work: real wearable input, offline AI guidance that learns each baseline, voice check-ins, and validation with clinicians and NASA standards.
